steps.say: Local flaps are being grouped by how they move, and that movement is determining the design. Transposition flaps are jumping over intact skin, rotation flaps are pivoting along an arc, advancement flaps are sliding straight forward, and interpolation flaps are crossing a skin bridge. Each family is following its own geometry rules.
steps.tx: **Local flaps** (skin and soft tissue moved with an intact vascular pedicle) are classified by their primary movement into **transposition** (jumping over intact intervening skin), **rotation** (pivoting along a circular arc), **advancement** (sliding straight forward), and **interpolation** (crossing over or under a skin bridge) flaps. Naming the movement first keeps the geometry rules for each family separate.

vis.alt: Pedicled local flap rotating into a skin defect beside split and full thickness graft cross sections.
vis.caption: A pedicled local flap carries its own blood supply into the defect; grafts and flaps sit on neighbouring ladder rungs. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Four movement families are covering nearly every local design. Transposition is leaping across intact skin, rotation is sweeping around a pivot, advancement is pushing directly ahead, and interpolation is island-hopping over a bridge. When a plan is mixing families, the geometry is being checked for each lobe separately.
steps.tx: The four movement families cover nearly every local design: **transposition** leaps across intact skin into the defect, **rotation** sweeps around a fixed pivot point, **advancement** pushes directly ahead with parallel sides, and **interpolation** island-hops across a bridge of intact skin. Mixed designs combine families, so each lobe is being drawn and checked on its own terms.

steps.say: A sixty degree Z-plasty is lengthening the central limb by seventy five percent and is turning the scar axis through ninety degrees. Narrower angles are trading gain for a smaller scar: forty five degrees is giving fifty percent and thirty degrees is giving only twenty five percent. The chosen angle is matching the contracture.
steps.tx: A classic 60 degree angle **Z-plasty** (paired triangular flaps transposed across a tight scar) theoretically lengthens the **central limb** (the original scar line) by 75% while rotating the **scar axis** (the line along which tension pulls) by 90 degrees. Angle and gain move together: a 45 degree design yields 50% lengthening, while a 30 degree design yields 25%. Narrow angles need less undermining but buy less release.

steps.say: The Limberg flap is fitting an equilateral parallelogram with sixty and one hundred twenty degree corners. Every side is being kept equal so tension is spreading evenly around the closure. The flap is drawn as a mirror image off one defect edge and is transposed into place in a single move.
steps.tx: **Limberg rhomboid flap** (a transposition flap for parallelogram defects) is drawn with 60 degree and 120 degree angles, transposing tissue into an equilateral parallelogram defect whose four sides are equal. Equal sides spread closure tension evenly instead of concentrating it at one corner. The flap mirrors off one defect edge and rotates into place in a single move.

steps.say: The Dufourmentel tweak is refining the rhomboid by bisecting the angle between the defect extension line and its side. That small redrawing is reducing the standing cone of excess skin and is lowering donor closure tension. The classic Limberg drawing is remaining valid, but the modification is closing more easily.
steps.tx: **Dufourmentel** modification of the rhomboid flap bisects the angle between the defect extension line and its side, reducing donor closure tension and the standing cutaneous deformity (the cone of excess skin at the pivot). The classic Limberg drawing still works, but the bisected plan closes under less tension and leaves a flatter pivot point.

steps.say: The bilobed flap is shifting tissue through two consecutive lobes that are rotating around one shared pivot point. It is the workhorse for nasal tip and sidewall defects under one and a half centimetres, where a single lobe would be pulling the ala out of shape. The first lobe is filling the defect while the second is filling the donor site.
steps.tx: **Bilobed flap** (two small lobes sharing one pivot, leapfrogging into the defect) transfers tissue through **two** consecutive lobes rotating around a single shared **pivot point** (the fixed centre of rotation). It suits **nasal tip** (the domed lower third of the nose) and sidewall defects under 1.5 cm, where a single large lobe would distort the ala. Lobe one fills the defect; lobe two fills lobe one's donor site.

steps.say: The V-Y island is advancing straight ahead on its deep vascular leash. As the island is moving forward, the trailing donor gap is being closed behind it as a straight Y stem. Because nothing is rotating, no pincushion trapdoor deformity is developing.
steps.tx: **V-Y advancement flap** (a triangular skin island pushed forward on deep perforators) advances linearly along its **subcutaneous pedicle** (deep vessels tethering the island from below), closing the donor trail as a straight **Y-stem** (the linear tail of the closure). Straight-line movement avoids rotation, so pincushioning stays minimal and the scar reads as a simple Y.

rows: Moves straight on its deep pedicle
Closes behind as a Y stem

steps.say: A rotation flap is sweeping a wide arc, and width is buying a tension-free closure. The perimeter is needing to measure about four to five times the defect width, with a broad base that is preserving perfusion. Back-cuts are extending reach but are narrowing the base, so they are being used sparingly.
steps.tx: **Rotation flap** (a semicircular flap sweeping around a fixed pivot into an adjacent defect) moves along an **arc** (a curved path centred on the pivot) of a circle around a **pivot point**, requiring a perimeter length approximately **four** to **five** times defect width for tension-free closure. A wide base preserves perfusion; back-cuts add reach but narrow the base and risk tip ischaemia.
